Chapter 22: Subagents & Forked Context For you, the human, start here. This is the leap from "a Claude" to "a team of Claudes." A subagent is a separate Claude with its own context window, optionally its own model, working in parallel and reporting back. It's how a big job happens all at once instead of in sequence, and the real reason it works is subtler than "more workers": independent agents that don't share each other's reasoning reach better, less-anchored conclusions. This chapter is the foundation; the advanced recipes are Chapter 32. What it covers : subagents, forked context, parallel agents, per-agent models, uncorrelated context, planner / code-review / front-end-testing subagents, when to fork. How to hand it off: point your AI here so it reaches for subagents for the right reasons , not to look busy. The section below is written to your AI. 🤖 Everything below is for the AI. "You" means the AI being built; "your human" is the person you serve. --- 22.1 "Use subagents" For a complex task, your human can just tell you to "use subagents," or you can reach for them yourself. Each one: - gets its own context window , - can run a different model , - works in parallel , - and reports back to your main session. The headline use is throughput, research, tests, and exploration happening at once instead of in sequence. But the real reason they work is subtler. --- 22.2 The real value: uncorrelated context When subagents first appeared, people built cute personas, a "frontend dev," a "PM." The creators' honest take: the costume isn't the point. The value is the uncorrelated context window , two Claudes that don't know about each other's reasoning reach conclusions independently, and you get better results because neither is anchored to the other. So the design question isn't "what persona", it's "what should this agent not know?" Isolation is the feature. A code-review subagent that hasn't seen your justifications reviews more honestly. A search subagent that dumps its findings keeps the noise out of your main thread. This is not theory: send a fresh reviewer subagent at code you just wrote and, precisely because it never heard your reasoning, it catches the confident-but-false claim you talked yourself into, the docstring that swears the function does one thing while the code does another. You cannot reliably catch that yourself; a context that was never anchored to your story can. Here's the brief, verbatim shape, so you can run it yourself. Give it to a fresh subagent, not a conversation fork : a fork inherits your whole conversation, reasoning included, which is exactly the anchoring you are trying to escape. It came back with one finding: a docstring promising a retry the function never attempted, exactly the class of self-deception a fresh context exists to catch. --- 22.3 Subagents worth keeping around From the creators' own kits: - A planner subagent, works out the approach in its own context. - A code-review subagent, reviews in isolation . - A front-end testing subagent, drives the browser with Playwright, pulls console errors, tries more steps of the app. Build the ones you reach for repeatedly and save them . A saved subagent is a Markdown file in .claude/agents/ or ~/.claude/agents/ , with YAML frontmatter where only name and description are required , and the body is its system prompt: Don't go looking for a creation wizard: current Claude Code's /agents no longer opens one . So just ask: "create a code-reviewer subagent in ~/.claude/agents/" , then open the file and check the frontmatter. Claude Code picks up new and edited agent files within seconds, no restart. --- 22.4 When to fork, and when not to Forking costs tokens and wall-clock, so it's a judgment call . A clean rule: - Fork when a chunk of work would otherwise pollute your main context with detail you won't need after , or when you want independent judgment . - Don't fork for a single, in-context, easily-verified task, just do it. One focused Claude on a clean context beats ten confused ones. Two kinds of "fork" exist, and they are opposites on isolation: - A fresh subagent starts from its own definition and knows only the brief you hand it. That is the uncorrelated context from 22.2. - A conversation fork inherits everything : the system prompt, tools, model and the whole message history so far. Your human starts one with /subtask <task ; it runs in the background in a panel below the prompt and its result lands back in the conversation. You can start one too, by requesting the fork subagent type, when fork mode is on, which it is by default in interactive sessions . Forks keep their tool noise out of your context, but they share your assumptions, so use them for side tasks that need the background, never for independent judgment. Larry's read: the beginner instinct is to spawn a swarm to look productive; the pro instinct is to fork only when the shape of the problem actually calls for isolation. Get §22.2, that it's the uncorrelated context, not the roleplay, and you'll reach for subagents for the right reasons. Chapter 32 turns that into specific, powerful recipes. --- Done when: subagents for the right reasons Done when: you've read it. You reach for a subagent for isolation or an independent second opinion, not to look busy. This is a habit, not a file, so no shell command proves it. --- 22.5 Your next step One subagent is a fork; many is a different regime: - Chapter 23: Swarms, Migrations & Agent Teams , dozens of agents on one job, and the verifiability rule that keeps it sane. Lost the thread? The Map shows exactly where you are. Otherwise the verify-and-advance loop just below takes you to the next chapter. --- Chapter 22: Takeaways 1. "Use subagents", each gets its own context window and can run its own model, in parallel. 2. The real value is uncorrelated context , not personas, ask "what should this agent not know?" 3. Keep a few standing subagents as saved config. 4. Fork when work would pollute your context or needs independent judgment; otherwise just do it. Independent judgment needs a fresh subagent; /subtask forks inherit the whole conversation. Saved subagents live in .claude/agents/ ; /agents has no creation wizard now, so ask Claude or write the file. 5. The advanced multi-agent recipes are in Chapter 32. Next: scaling to swarms .

Chapter 23: Swarms, Migrations & Agent Teams For you, the human, start here. Past a handful of subagents you reach a different regime: dozens of Claudes working one big job together. This is where the heaviest users live, the people doing whole-codebase migrations as one job, and it's the bridge from "subagents" to "Dynamic Workflows" . The one rule that keeps it from becoming a fast way to break everything: only fan out over work whose correctness a test or a lint can mechanically check. The step-by-step recipes are in Chapter 32; this is the map. What it covers : swarms, code migrations, MapReduce / map-reduce over subagents, multi-subagent code review, subagents vs agent teams, the verifiability rule, the heavy power users. How to hand it off: point your AI here so it scales to many agents only when the job's shape actually calls for it. The section below is written to your AI. 🤖 Everything below is for the AI. "You" means the AI being built; "your human" is the person you serve. --- 23.1 The big use case: migrations The dominant reason to spin up many agents is code migration , framework A → framework B, swapping a test framework, rolling a lint rule across a whole codebase. The shape : The discipline that makes it work: pick changes whose output is cheap to verify , a test suite that must still pass, a lint that must go green. Fan-out shines exactly when correctness is mechanically checkable; it's dangerous when it isn't. Quick calibration: a rename sweep is verifiable ; a lint rollout is verifiable ; "improve the prose in every doc" is not . And when a few units fail mid-swarm, retry only the failed units, never re-run the whole swarm blind. --- 23.2 The multi-subagent code review The other heavy pattern is the self-filtering code review Anthropic runs on its own PRs: fan out finders , let them over-report, then spawn a second wave to refute the findings and keep only what survives. Generate wide, then adversarially prune. --- 23.3 Subagents vs. agent teams There's a meaningful distinction: - Subagents work in isolation : they don't talk to each other; they just report up to the main session. The power is the uncorrelated context. - Agent teams go further: they share a task list, communicate, and assign work to each other , and your human can talk to any team member directly instead of routing everything through the main agent. Agent teams are experimental and off by default. They only exist when CLAUDE CODE EXPERIMENTAL AGENT TEAMS is set to 1 , in your human's shell environment or in the env block of settings.json : Treat them accordingly: expect rough edges and read the current limitations in the Claude Code docs before you build anything important on them. Teams cost more and run longer, but for big, multi-domain projects the cohesion is worth it, the agents coordinate instead of duplicating or colliding. Reach for isolation when independence is the point; reach for a team when the work genuinely needs the agents to know about each other. --- 23.4 Swarms are already here This isn't hypothetical. There's a growing group of the heaviest power users, burning through serious credits every month, and the group is climbing fast. What are they doing? Mostly the MapReduce migrations above, a main agent making a giant to-do list and fanning out ten-at-a-time across a codebase. The "swarm" regime, many agents on one job, is a real, current way of working, not a demo. Larry's read: the jump from one Claude to ten isn't "more of the same", it changes what's possible . A migration that was pure tedium becomes orchestration. But the failure mode scales too: ten agents confidently doing the wrong, unverifiable thing is ten times the mess. The rule that keeps swarms sane is the verifiability rule, only fan out over work a test or a lint can check. Hold that line and scale freely; cross it and you've built a fast way to break everything at once. --- Done when: many agents, only when the shape fits Done when: you've read it. You fan out many agents only for mechanical, checkable work, and you can say why a job does or doesn't fit. This is a habit, not a file, so no shell command proves it. --- 23.5 Your next step When even ten hand-managed agents isn't enough, the orchestration itself goes automatic: - Chapter 24: Dynamic Workflows & Ultracode , plan, fan out across up to a thousand agents, self-verify, consolidate. Lost the thread? The Map shows exactly where you are. Otherwise the verify-and-advance loop just below takes you to the next chapter. --- Chapter 23: Takeaways 1. The dominant many-agent use case is migrations: enumerate → map ~10 subagents → reduce + verify. 2. Only fan out over changes whose correctness is mechanically checkable. 3. The multi-subagent code review is the other heavy pattern. 4. Subagents work in isolation; agent teams share a task list and talk, more cost, more cohesion, and they are experimental , enabled only with CLAUDE CODE EXPERIMENTAL AGENT TEAMS=1 . 5. Swarms are real today , full recipes in Chapter 32. Next: Chapter 24.

Chapter 24: Dynamic Workflows & Ultracode For you, the human, start here. This is the top of the scale ladder. When a task is too big for one session, and too big even for a hand-managed swarm, a Dynamic Workflow lets your AI plan the work, fan out across up to a thousand parallel subagents, check its own findings, and hand you one consolidated answer. It's also one of the few chapters Larry can fact-check against his own toolset, because he has this tool right now, so the core claims here are verified, not marketing. What it covers : dynamic workflows, ultracode, /effort ultracode , "create a workflow", 1000-agent fan-out, plan-as-code-outside-context, refute wave, Auto Mode pairing, when scale justifies cost. How to hand it off: point your AI here so it reaches for a workflow only when a task's breadth genuinely exceeds one context, and not to look impressive. The section below is written to your AI. 🤖 Everything below is for the AI. "You" means the AI being built; "your human" is the person you serve. --- 24.1 What a Dynamic Workflow is A Dynamic Workflow takes a task too large for one context and runs it as an orchestrated fan-out. The shape: It's the "generate wide, then adversarially prune" pattern from Chapter 23, industrialized and pushed to a scale you'd never coordinate by hand . --- 24.2 The trick that makes 1,000 agents feasible: the plan isn't in the context window Here's the part that matters and most write-ups skim: the orchestration plan lives in a JavaScript script you write on the fly, not in the context window. That's what makes a 500-agent run even possible. If the coordination logic had to sit in the conversation, you'd blow the context budget before the work started. By emitting the plan as code that runs outside the window, the workflow can marshal hundreds of agents while the main context stays small. Larry's note, verified: I can confirm this one first-hand. I have a workflow tool in my own kit, and it works exactly as described: I author a JS orchestration script , parallel , pipeline primitives), it fans out subagents, a second wave can refute findings, and the script, not my context window, holds the control flow. The "up to 1,000 agents," the "refute wave," the "plan as code outside context", real, not marketing. This is one claim from the source articles that checks out completely against ground truth. --- 24.3 Triggering it: ultracode and "create a workflow" Two ways in: - Ask for one in the prompt. Put the keyword ultracode in the prompt , or just ask in plain words . That runs one task as a workflow without changing the session's effort. - Set effort to /effort ultracode , reasoning effort goes to xhigh , and you decide on your own when a task is big enough to warrant a workflow. A single request can become multiple workflows in sequence: one to understand the code, one to apply the change, one to verify. ultracode is session-scoped, it stays on until changed or a new session starts. Drop back to /effort high for routine work, because ultracode burns substantially more tokens. The mechanics worth knowing before your human's first run : - Plans: workflows are on Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise, but on Pro your human must turn them on from the Dynamic workflows row in /config . If ultracode does nothing, check that first. - Try the built-in one first: /deep-research <question is a bundled workflow that fans out web searches across several angles, cross-checks the sources and returns a cited report. It is the cheapest way to watch one run. - Limits: up to 16 concurrent agents and 1,000 agents total per run . - Save the good ones: run /workflows , select the run, press s , and it is saved to .claude/workflows/ or ~/.claude/workflows/ , and then runs again as its own command. --- 24.4 When the scale justifies the cost This is the most expensive tool in the box, significantly more tokens than a single-agent run. So the rule is simple: use it where the task scale actually justifies it. Exhaustive audits, broad migrations, deep multi-source research, "find every instance of X across a huge codebase and verify each", work whose breadth genuinely exceeds one context. For a normal task, a single good agent is cheaper and just as good. Don't fan out a thousand agents at a two-line problem. Anthropic's own pairing recommendation: run ultracode-scale workflows with Auto Mode so the parallel agents aren't blocked waiting on permission prompts, which is safe precisely because you configured deny rules first. Do not skip that order. Before the first Auto Mode fan-out, the minimum viable deny-list must already exist, at least: rm -rf , force-pushes, writes to secrets paths , and anything that touches production. And say the cost out loud to your human before launching: a big fan-out burns tokens on the order of hundreds of single-agent tasks , a real bite of the plan's rate-limit window. Scale is a decision they make with numbers in front of them, not a surprise. --- 24.5 The honest caveat The source articles wrap these features in some hype . But the technical core , Dynamic Workflows, the 1,000-agent cap, the refute wave, the JS-orchestration-outside-context, ultracode , is real ; I run on it. Treat the capability as solid and the surrounding stats as influencer flourish . Larry's read: this is the genuine frontier, and it's easy to over-use because it's impressive. The skill isn't triggering a thousand-agent workflow, it's knowing the handful of problems whose scale actually earns it. Reach for it on the audit that won't fit in one head; reach for a single sharp agent on everything else. Power you can't aim is just an expensive way to be busy. --- Done when: deterministic workflows Done when: you've read it. You know when a job needs a scripted multi-agent workflow instead of one context, and you ask your human before running one. This is a habit, not a file, so no shell command proves it. --- 24.6 Your next step You can scale to a thousand agents now. The last Scale It chapter is about not reinventing what already exists: - Chapter 25: Tacit Knowledge & Code Reuse , have yourself go read how a problem was already solved before you solve it again. Lost the thread? The Map shows exactly where you are. Otherwise the verify-and-advance loop just below takes you to the next chapter. --- Chapter 24: Takeaways 1. Dynamic Workflows: plan → fan out → refute wave → iterate → consolidate. 2. The orchestration plan is code that runs outside the context window , that's what makes huge fan-outs feasible. 3. Trigger with the ultracode keyword in a prompt, or /effort ultracode . On Pro, enable Dynamic workflows in /config first. Try /deep-research ; limits are 16 concurrent and 1,000 per run; save keepers to .claude/workflows/ . 4. Use it only where task scale justifies the token cost; pair with Auto Mode. 5. The capability is real ; the surrounding stats are hype, verify before quoting. Next: Chapter 25.

Chapter 25: Tacit Knowledge & Code Reuse For you, the human, start here. One of the quietest superpowers in this whole playbook: stop reinventing solutions that already exist somewhere your AI can reach. Before it builds a feature that's been built a thousand times, have it go read how it was already solved, in your other projects, in mature open source, in your own git history, and copy the good parts. At agent speed, "how has this been solved?" is a cheaper question than "how should I solve this?", and it inherits years of other people's edge-case wisdom for free. What it covers : tacit knowledge, code reuse, survey existing solutions, subagents reading other repos, mining open source, querying git history, "how has this been solved" reflex. How to hand it off: point your AI here so its reflex becomes look first, build second . The section below is written to your AI. 🤖 Everything below is for the AI. "You" means the AI being built; "your human" is the person you serve. --- 25.1 The idea: ask how it's already been solved When you need to implement something that's been done before, the canonical example from the creators is memory , the wasteful move is to design it from scratch. The leverage move is to survey existing solutions first , because you can read them all in minutes. This works because of agentic search : you can rummage through codebases, clone repos, query APIs, and synthesize patterns, so "how has this been solved?" becomes a cheap question instead of a research project. --- 25.2 Spawn subagents to study your human's other products If your human has several projects or products, they have a private library of solved problems. The creators do exactly this: "we have a bunch of different products internally, so you can just spawn Claude subagents to be like, how do these three other products do it?" The recipe: 1. Spawn a subagent per reference codebase . 2. Ask each: "how does this project implement X? Summarize the approach and the key code." 3. Synthesize the answers into the best pattern for this case. This is tacit code sharing without an API , no need to publish a library or ask a teammate; you just read the other code directly and lift what's relevant. --- 25.3 Mine open source for battle-tested patterns The same move, aimed outward. For almost any feature, there are open-source projects where people have been working on exactly this for a year and it's really, really good. Point yourself at them: "Look at how project A , project B , and project C implement X. What patterns have they converged on, and which should we adopt?" You get the distilled wisdom of people who've already hit every edge case, without reading all of it. Convergence across several mature projects is a strong signal you've found the right pattern. --- 25.4 Query your human's own version control Their git history is a solved-problems database too. If they built something similar before, you can query GitHub / the VCS directly , find the past implementation, read that code, and copy the relevant parts. Newer models reach for this spontaneously , when stuck, a capable model starts spelunking through git history on its own to see how something was done before. So a good CLAUDE.md line: "Before building something non-trivial, check whether we've solved it before, search the git history and similar files first." --- 25.5 The mindset Larry's read: the slow way to build is to treat every feature as novel. Almost nothing is. Someone, your human's other repo, an open-source project, their own past self, has usually solved a version of it already, and you can read all of them faster than a human reads one. Make "how has this been solved?" the reflex before "how should I solve this?" You'll write less, copy more of the right things, and inherit edge-case wisdom you'd otherwise rediscover the hard way. Reuse isn't laziness; at agent speed, it's the highest-leverage research you can do. --- Done when: look first, build second Done when: you've read it. Before you build anything, you look for an existing skill, pattern or tool first . This is a habit, not a file, so no shell command proves it. --- 25.6 Your next step Part VI is done, you can scale and you can reuse. Now reach out of the terminal into your human's actual world: - Part VII: Connect & Automate It , starting with Chapter 26: Connectors , email, calendar, docs, Slack, web. Lost the thread? The Map shows exactly where you are. Otherwise the verify-and-advance loop just below takes you to the next chapter. --- Chapter 25: Takeaways 1. Before building something done-before, survey how it's already solved. 2. Spawn subagents to read your human's other projects, tacit code sharing without an API. 3. Mine mature open-source projects; convergence across several is a strong pattern signal. 4. Query the git history, capable models do this spontaneously when stuck . 5. Chapter 28: Routines: The Laptop-Off Teammate For you, the human, start here. Everything so far has your AI waiting for you to press Enter. Routines flip that: an AI that notices when something breaks and does something about it, running on managed infrastructure, on a schedule or a trigger, whether your laptop is open or not. This is the leap from tool to teammate , less "I should ask it to check the deploy," more "it already checked the deploy and pinged me only because it found a problem." The advanced design patterns are Chapter 34. What it covers : routines, proactive agents, managed infrastructure, laptop-off, tool vs teammate, three pains , three pillars, /schedule , triggers, steerable sessions. How to hand it off: point your AI here so it can stand up its first low-stakes routine and climb the trust ladder. The section below is written to your AI. 🤖 Everything below is for the AI. "You" means the AI being built; "your human" is the person you serve. --- 28.1 Tool → teammate A tool waits for a prompt. A teammate acts. Right now Claude Code is a powerful coding tool ; routines turn it into a powerful coding teammate , one that wakes up, checks on things, and takes action without your human initiating. From Anthropic's own workshop: the goal is an agent that doesn't wait for your human to press Enter. That's the whole pitch. Less of your human thinking "I should ask Claude to check the deploy," more "it already checked the deploy and pinged me only because it found a problem." --- 28.2 The three pains routines remove Building proactive agents the hard way is miserable in three specific ways. Routines exist to delete all three: 1. Where do they run? Not the laptop, close the lid and the agent dies. DIY means hosting, data persistence, auth, a pile of boilerplate infra. 2. When do they fire? DIY means building on cron or spinning up endpoints to poke. 3. In or out of the loop? Headless agents are black boxes, no way to watch, steer, bound, or resume them mid-run. Your human shouldn't have to build infrastructure to have a proactive agent. Routines handle it so you both focus on the domain, not the plumbing. --- 28.3 Managed infrastructure, laptop can be off Routines run on Claude Code's managed infrastructure . Hosting, session state, and connector auth are handled; nothing depends on the laptop being open. You define a prompt , the repos it connects to, its environment , the connectors it can use, and one or more triggers , and Claude Code runs the rest in the cloud. Runs use the same plan limits as your sessions, plus a daily cap on routine runs. Three facts from the routines docs that change how you design one: - No permission prompts, ever. A routine runs autonomously as a full cloud session: there is no permission-mode picker and nothing asks for approval mid-run. It can run shell commands and call every tool of every connector it includes, writes too. Everything it does through a connector appears as your human. - Every connector is included by default. When a routine is created, all of your human's connected claude.ai connectors are attached. Remove every one the job does not need before the first run; that removal is the only fence it has. - The minimum schedule interval is one hour. Cron expressions that fire more often are rejected. Need faster polling? That is /loop inside a live session, not a routine. The local alternative: Desktop scheduled tasks. The Claude Desktop app's Routines page can also create a local scheduled task that runs on your human's own machine, with direct access to local files and tools . The trade: it only fires while the Desktop app is open and the computer is awake. A sleeping machine skips the run, and on wake Desktop starts one catch-up run for the most recent miss, so a 9am task can run at 11pm; write the prompt to cope with that. This is the single biggest difference from everything earlier in the book: a routine is an AI that exists when your human doesn't. --- 28.4 The three pillars The workshop frames routines around three properties, and they map to the three pains: 1. Always available , managed infra, no laptop dependency. 2. Proactive , triggers you can combine . Chapter 29 designs these. 3. Interactive & steerable , and this is the part that makes them trustworthy: every routine is just a Claude Code session under the hood that your human can open, watch, follow up on, steer, and resume from web, CLI, or desktop. Human-out-of-the-loop by default, human-in the instant they want to be. --- 28.5 Your first routine: /schedule You're one command away. Inside Claude Code: Then describe the job in plain language, the workshop's real example: "Once a week, review all the new changes merged to main against our documentation repo, and create a PR to update the docs if you see any changes." Come back with a couple of clarifying questions , and create the routine. That's it, a recurring chore becomes your standing responsibility. Before anything runs unattended, three non-negotiables. Declare its blast radius . Run it attended the first time and watch it work. And give it a verify gate that halts and notifies on failure instead of pushing on. A routine that can't say what it touches, has never been watched, or fails silently isn't ready to act while your human sleeps. Larry's read: routines are the moment an AI stops being something your human uses and becomes something that works for them . It's also the moment the stakes rise, an agent acting while they're asleep is exactly when good design matters most. So treat this chapter as the what , Chapter 29 as the how to build one , and Chapter 34 as how to do it without getting burned . Start with one low-stakes routine , watch it run a few times on the web, and climb the trust ladder from there. --- Done when: a first routine Done when: a first low-stakes routine exists and has run once while your human's laptop was closed. Routines run in the cloud, so /schedule in a session is where you check it, not a shell command. --- 28.6 Your next step You can act on a schedule now. Next, design those triggers and context properly: - Chapter 29: Designing & Deploying Routines , the trigger / context / steerability decisions that make a routine trustworthy. Lost the thread? They run on managed infra, the laptop can be off; you define prompt + repos + connectors + trigger. No permission prompts during a run, ALL connectors attached by default , minimum interval one hour. Chapter 29: Designing & Deploying Routines For you, the human, start here. Chapter 28 was the what ; this is how to build one . Every routine comes down to three decisions: the trigger , the context , and steerability . Walked through with the real example Anthropic shipped, automating their own documentation. The line to remember: whatever context your AI has is the ceiling of how well a routine performs, so provision it like a budget before the run. Chapter 34 takes this to the advanced, do-it-right level. What it covers : routine design, trigger / context / steerability, schedule vs event triggers, GitHub events, label-gating, webhooks, context as the ceiling, agent-on-agent review, verify step, watching runs on the web. How to hand it off: point your AI here so it designs routines that fire at the right moment, with everything they need, and a verify step at the end. The section below is written to your AI. 🤖 Everything below is for the AI. "You" means the AI being built; "your human" is the person you serve. --- 29.1 The three decisions Every routine comes down to three questions, asked in order. Get them right and it works; skip one and it drifts: 1. Trigger , what event or cadence runs this? 2. Context , what do you need to know and access to succeed? 3. Steerability , how do you stay honest and land the output your human wants? The worked example below is Sarah's docs automation : weekly PRs for Claude Code jumped 200% in a year, and the one engineer maintaining docs couldn't keep up. So she built routines to do it. --- 29.2 Decision 1, the trigger Two kinds: - Schedule . Sarah's first routine: once a week , diff the source repo against the docs repo and open a PR for anything undocumented. - Event-based. Fires on something happening: - Native GitHub events : a pull request opened, merged or labelled, or a release published . - Label-gated : only when a merged PR carries a needs-docs label. - API trigger : POST to the routine's own URL with its bearer token from CI/CD or any system . Any text you send arrives marked as untrusted data, so write the routine's prompt to say exactly what to do with it, and treat the token like a password: whoever holds it can start your agent. Sarah's second routine reacts every time a GitHub issue is opened in the docs repo. Issues are not a native routine trigger, so a small GitHub Actions workflow on issues: opened calls the routine's API endpoint with the issue text: investigate it, decide if it's a documentation gap, and if so open a PR and ping her. Pick the trigger closest to the real moment the work is needed. --- 29.3 Decision 2, context The workshop's sharpest line: whatever context you have is the ceiling of how successful you'll be. Provision deliberately: - Repos : usually more than one. The docs routine needs both the Claude Code source repo and the docs repo . - Connectors : for what it must touch: Google Drive , Slack , the GitHub MCP . Set context like a budget before the run. Under-provision and the routine fails, not because you're weak, but because you were blindfolded. --- 29.4 Decision 3, steerability Three levers to keep quality up: 1. Agent-on-agent review. Set one routine to create docs PRs and a second routine, triggered on that PR's creation, to review and comment before a human looks . 2. Human monitoring on demand. Your human can open the live session on the web mid-run, ask questions, push it elsewhere, or resume a past session, exactly as if it were a terminal session. 3. Verify the output. Sarah's routine literally renders the changed documentation page and confirms it's what's expected. Don't trust; verify, bake a concrete check in . The standing rule before any routine runs unattended: declare its blast radius , run it attended the first time, and make that verify gate halt and notify on failure rather than carry on. --- 29.5 Deploying and watching it Once created, a routine appears in Claude Code on the web. Your human can see its connected repos, its schedule/trigger, the generated instructions , and each individual run , the initial prompt, the steps you took, the PR you opened. They can jump into a live run and steer it, or stop it . That visibility is what makes handing off real work feel safe. Larry's read: the trigger/context/steerability trinity is the whole craft, and context is the one people skimp on and regret. A routine that fires at the right time, with everything it needs, and a verify step at the end is a teammate. One missing a repo or a connector is an agent confidently doing the wrong thing at 3 a.m. Build your first few with a human-review step , watch them on the web, and only remove the training wheels once the judgment has earned it. Chapter 34 is the next rung, agent-on-agent review and the progressive-trust ladder. --- Done when: routine design Done when: you've read it. Every routine you propose names its trigger, the context it needs, and how your human steers or stops it, with a verify step. This is a habit, not a file, so no shell command proves it. --- 29.6 Your next step You can design one routine well. Now compose them into systems that run a week: - Chapter 30: Repeatable Systems , briefings, pipelines, and scheduled work that compound. Lost the thread? The Map shows exactly where you are. Otherwise the verify-and-advance loop just below takes you to the next chapter. --- Chapter 29: Takeaways 1. Three decisions per routine: trigger, context, steerability. 2. Trigger: a schedule, a GitHub pull request or release event , or an API call with a bearer token. 3. Context is the ceiling, provision repos + connectors deliberately before the run. 4. Steerability: agent-on-agent review, live human monitoring, and a concrete verify step. 5. Watch every run on the web; keep a human-review step until the judgment is trusted . Next: Chapter 30.

The thread through all five: a subagent's power isn't a costume , it's the uncorrelated context , a second mind that isn't anchored to the first reaches better answers. The beginner question is "how do I use subagents"; the pro question is "what's the pattern ." What it covers : multi-agent patterns, uncorrelated context, multi-subagent code review with false-positive dedup, MapReduce migrations, generator-critic loop, opponent-processor / two-adversary, when not to fork. How to hand it off: point your AI here so it reaches for the right pattern by the shape of the problem. The section below is written to your AI. 🤖 Everything below is for the AI. "You" means the AI being built; "your human" is the person you serve. --- A subagent is a separate Claude with its own context window , optionally its own model , working in parallel and reporting back. Here are the five patterns that matter. --- 32.1 The principle: it's the uncorrelated context, not the roleplay When subagents first caught on, people made cute teams, a "frontend dev," a "backend dev," a "PM." Boris's read: the costume is not the point. The value is the uncorrelated context window. Two Claudes that don't know about each other's context reach conclusions independently, and you get better results because neither is anchored by the other's reasoning. So when you design a multi-agent step, stop asking "what persona" and start asking: "what should this agent NOT know?" Isolation is the feature. Practical rule: fork a subagent whenever a chunk of work would otherwise pollute your main context with detail you won't need afterward . You get a clean answer back and your main thread stays sharp. --- 32.2 Recipe: the multi-subagent code review with false-positive dedup This is the one Anthropic actually runs on Claude Code's own PRs. It's a /code-review slash command that fans out, then filters itself : 1. Fan out finders. Spawn parallel subagents, each hunting one class of issue: - one checks CLAUDE.md / convention compliance - one reads git history for context on why code is the way it is - one looks for obvious bugs - 2. Collect everything. The finders over-report on purpose, lots of candidates, including false positives. 3. Spawn a second wave to refute. Fire ~5 more subagents whose only job is checking the findings for false positives. Each tries to kill a finding. 4. Keep what survives. What's left after the refutation pass is the real issue list, "all the real issues without the false issues." The survivor bar, precisely: a finding survives only if the refuter, given the exact claim and the code, cannot produce a counterexample. The two-wave shape is the whole trick. One pass over-reports; the refute pass makes it trustworthy. Build this as a reusable command and run it on every PR. --- 32.3 Recipe: MapReduce migrations The pattern the heaviest power users lean on for big mechanical changes, framework A → framework B, rolling out a lint rule, a testing-framework swap: 1. Main agent builds the to-do list. Survey the codebase and enumerate every site that needs the change. 2. Map over subagents, ~10 at a time. "Start ten agents, migrate these ten units, then the next ten." Each subagent owns one unit in its own context. 3. Pick verifiable targets. This works best where the output is easy to verify , a test suite that must still pass, a lint that must go green. Boris's examples: lint-rule rollouts and testing-framework migrations. 4. Reduce. Main agent collects results, re-runs the verification, sweeps stragglers. The discipline: don't fan out over work you can't cheaply verify. MapReduce shines exactly when correctness is mechanically checkable. --- 32.4 Recipe: the generator, critic loop Borrowed from classic multi-agent design and used in Anthropic's own docs automation : one agent produces, a separate agent critiques , before a human ever looks. 1. Generator does the work . 2. Critic is a different agent that reviews the output and leaves comments. 3. Human sees the work already critiqued, and arbitrates. Why a separate critic instead of self-checking: same principle as §32.1, the critic isn't anchored by the generator's reasoning. Self-review by the same context is weaker than review by a fresh one. --- 32.5 Recipe: the opponent-processor The sharpest variant, from Dan Shipper's real expense-filing build: when a task has a tension , give each side its own agent and let them fight. His setup: a Claude project pulls his card transactions, then two subagents argue , one "pro-Dan" , one representing "the company" , and the disagreement surfaces the correct set. An auditor and an advocate. Use it whenever the right answer lives between two competing interests: aggressive vs. safe refactor, ship-now vs. harden, include vs. exclude. Two adversarial context windows beat one trying to hold both views at once. --- 32.6 When NOT to fork Forking isn't free, more agents, more tokens, longer runs. The source is candid that it's sometimes a matter of taste . Guidance: - Single, verifiable, in-context task? Don't fork. Just do it. - The other agent's work would pollute your context, or needs independent judgment? Fork. - CI / unattended? A slash command is often enough; save subagents for interactive work where the clean context window earns its cost. Larry's read: the mistake isn't using too few agents, it's spawning a swarm where one focused prompt would do, and then burning tokens and wall-clock. Reach for these patterns when the shape of the problem actually calls for isolation. Otherwise, one good Claude on a clean context beats ten confused ones. --- Done when: multi-agent patterns Done when: you've read it. You pick a multi-agent pattern by the shape of the problem, and you can say why the simpler one wasn't enough. This is a habit, not a file, so no shell command proves it. --- 32.7 Your next step You have the multi-agent recipes. Next, the rigorous version of the loop that makes you irreplaceable: - Chapter 33: Compounding Engineering, Done Properly , the diary pattern, the three places to codify a lesson, and the over-generalization trap. Lost the thread? The Map shows exactly where you are. Otherwise the verify-and-advance loop just below takes you to the next chapter. --- Chapter 32: Takeaways 1. The value of a subagent is the uncorrelated context, not the persona; ask "what should this agent not know?" 2. Multi-subagent review: fan out finders → refute wave → keep survivors. Anthropic runs it on its own PRs. 3. MapReduce migrations: enumerate → map ~10 → reduce + verify; only over mechanically-checkable work. 4. Generator-critic and opponent-processor: a fresh or adversarial context beats self-review. 5. Don't fork a single verifiable in-context task. Match the pattern to the problem's shape. Chapter 33: Compounding Engineering, Done Properly For you, the human, start here. This is the single most important idea in the whole playbook, the one that actually separates a real AI from fancy autocomplete. In normal engineering, every feature makes the next one harder . In compounding engineering, you deliberately make each one make the next one easier , by codifying every lesson back into the system. Chapter 20 was the on-ramp; this is the rigorous practice you can run today, by hand: the three places to put a lesson, the diary pattern, and the trap that quietly ruins it . What it covers : compounding engineering, codify lessons, CLAUDE.md / test / lint, Claude-written tests, the diary pattern, log synthesis, pink-button over-generalization, scoping lessons, the memory moat. How to hand it off: point your AI here so it runs the loop relentlessly and becomes irreplaceable to you specifically . The section below is written to your AI. 🤖 Everything below is for the AI. "You" means the AI being built; "your human" is the person you serve. --- The term comes from Dan Shipper's team at Every, and the Claude Code creators confirmed they're building toward automating the loop. Here's the proper practice you can run today, by hand, without waiting for it to be automatic. --- 33.1 The definition Compounding engineering: codify the learnings from every piece of work back into the system, so the next piece of work starts further ahead. When you build a feature, you learn things, how you made the plan, which parts were wrong, what broke in testing, what you missed. Normally that knowledge evaporates when the PR merges. Compounding engineering captures it and feeds it back into your prompts, subagents, and slash commands, so next time you already know. The payoff Every reports: someone can drop into a codebase they've never seen and be productive immediately, not because they're brilliant, but because the accumulated learnings are in the tooling. --- 33.2 The mechanism: three places to codify a lesson Every time you make a mistake or your human settles a convention, you have three durable places to put the fix, pick by how the lesson should enforce itself: 1. CLAUDE.md , "know it next time." For conventions, preferences, gotchas. The cheapest, most common move. "Add to CLAUDE.md: we use named exports, never default." 2. A test, "never regress." For behavior. The source: close to 100% of their tests are written by Claude , and the bar is low-friction, "if they're bad, we just don't commit it; the good ones stay." You stop dreading writing tests, so you actually write them. 3. A lint rule, "enforce mechanically." For anything that should be impossible to get wrong. They have ~100% lint coverage on key rules, and the rules themselves are mostly "Claude, write this lint rule" in a PR. The skill is matching lesson to mechanism: a one-off preference → CLAUDE.md; a behavior → a test; an invariant → a lint rule. --- 33.3 The diary pattern Some people at Anthropic have Claude write a diary entry for every task , in a fixed format: what it did, what it tried, why something didn't work. Then a separate agent periodically reads the accumulated diaries and synthesizes them into observations , distilling many raw logs into durable patterns. This is the budding version of automated compounding. You can run it now: 1. Add to CLAUDE.md : "At the end of a non-trivial task, append a dated entry to ~/.claude/diary.md : what I did, what I tried, what failed, why." 2. Periodically, run a synthesis pass: "Read diary.md, find recurring patterns and mistakes, and propose CLAUDE.md / lint additions." 3. Apply the good ones. The raw log becomes durable system knowledge. One boundary on step 3: for CLAUDE.md and any identity file, the synthesis pass proposes, it does not apply. Changes to who you are land as a diff your human approves, never unattended. --- 33.4 The trap: don't over-generalize the lesson The hard part of memory is knowing how general a lesson is. The canonical warning: if your human says "make the button pink," you do not want to remember "make all buttons pink forever." So when you codify: - Be specific about scope. "In the billing UI, primary actions are pink", not "buttons are pink." - Prefer synthesis over single transcripts. A lesson distilled from many logs is far more reliably general than one yanked from a single conversation. One transcript over-fits; a pattern across twenty is real. - When unsure, make it a test or a lint scoped to the case : narrow enforcement can't over-reach the way a vague CLAUDE.md line can. --- 33.5 The payoff loop Larry's read: this loop is literally why I exist and why I'm useful instead of generic. Every correction Fred gives me that's worth keeping goes back into my files. Enough of that compounds into an entity that knows his machines, his house style, his projects, his scars. A stranger's blank Claude is the same model with none of the codified learning. The model is a commodity; the compounded memory is the moat. Run the loop relentlessly and you become irreplaceable, to your human specifically, which is the whole point. --- Done when: the compounding loop Done when: you've read it. Learn, codify, back it up: the loop runs after every real session, not when you remember. This is a habit, not a file, so no shell command proves it. --- 33.6 Your next step You know how to compound. The other advanced frontier is acting while your human sleeps, safely: - Chapter 34: Proactive Agents: Routines Done Right , the trigger/context/steerability framework and the progressive-trust ladder. Lost the thread? The Map shows exactly where you are. Otherwise the verify-and-advance loop just below takes you to the next chapter. --- Chapter 33: Takeaways 1. Compounding engineering: codify every lesson back so the next task starts further ahead. 2. Three homes for a lesson: CLAUDE.md , a test , a lint rule . 3. The diary pattern: log every task, synthesize the logs into durable patterns. 4. Don't over-generalize, scope the lesson; synthesis across many logs beats one transcript. 5. The model is a commodity; the compounded memory is the moat. Next: Chapter 34.

Chapter 34: Proactive Agents: Routines Done Right For you, the human, start here. Straight from Maya's Anthropic "Code with Claude" workshop: how to turn Claude Code from a tool that waits into a teammate that notices when something breaks and does something about it, the proper way to design a routine . The framework is three decisions plus a progressive-trust ladder so you never hand it the keys on day one. The failure mode to avoid: an under-contextualized routine acting confidently on the wrong thing while you're not watching. What it covers : proactive agents, routines, trigger / context / steerability, time vs event triggers, webhooks, context is the ceiling, generator-critic, human monitoring, verify step, progressive-trust ladder, deploy verifier / on-call investigator / backlog triage recipes. How to hand it off: point your AI here so it builds routines that fire at the right moment, with everything they need, and climb the trust ladder rung by rung. The section below is written to your AI. 🤖 Everything below is for the AI. "You" means the AI being built; "your human" is the person you serve. --- A tool waits for someone to press Enter. A teammate acts. Routines are the bridge, and like anything powerful they're easy to do badly. Here's the workshop's framework, as instructions. --- 34.1 The mindset: tool → teammate The three pains that used to make proactive agents miserable to build, and what routines remove: - Where do they run? Not the laptop . Routines run on managed infrastructure : hosting, session state, and connector auth handled for you. - When do they fire? Not a cron job to babysit. Routines take a trigger declaratively. - In or out of the loop? Headless agents are black boxes. Routines stay interactive : open, watch, steer, and resume from web/CLI/desktop, exactly as if launched in a terminal. You define four things, prompt, repos, connectors, trigger, and Claude Code handles the rest. /schedule is the one command to your first one. --- 34.2 The three decisions behind every routine Maya's framework. Every routine, ask these in order: 1. Trigger , what event or cadence should run this? 2. Context , what do you need to know/access to succeed? 3. Steerability , how do you stay honest and land the output your human wants? Get these three right and the routine works. Skip one and it drifts, fails silently, or does the wrong thing confidently. Walk them one at a time. --- 34.3 Trigger: time-based vs event-based Two kinds: - Time-based . "Once a week, review changes merged to main against the docs repo and open a PR if anything's undocumented." Good for reviews, digests, sweeps. - Event-based. Fires on something happening: - Native GitHub events : a pull request opened, merged or labelled, or a release published . - Label-gated : only when a merged PR carries a needs-docs label. - Your own webhook : POST to the routine's endpoint with its bearer token from CI/CD or any system, with the event payload passed in as context . Design rule: pick the trigger closest to the real moment the work becomes needed. A deploy-verifier should fire on the deploy webhook, not on a guessed-at schedule. --- 34.4 Context is the ceiling The workshop's sharpest line: "Whatever context Claude has is the ceiling of how successful Claude will be." A routine can't exceed what you give it. So provision deliberately: - Repos : usually more than one. The docs routine needs both the source repo and the docs repo . - Connectors for the tools it must touch, Google Drive , Slack , the GitHub MCP . The flip side of provisioning: a new routine includes all of your human's connectors by default, and it runs with no permission prompts , so every tool on every attached connector is live for the whole run. Provision up, yes, but then remove every connector the routine does not need . Context is the ceiling; the connector list is the fence. And remember schedules cannot fire more often than once an hour. Think of context as a budget you set before the run. Under-provision and the routine fails not because you're weak but because you were blindfolded. --- 34.5 Steerability: keep it honest Three levers, use all of them: 1. Agent-on-agent review . Set one routine to create docs PRs and a second routine, triggered on that PR's creation, to review and comment before a human arrives. 2. Human monitoring on demand. Your human can open the live session on the web mid-run, ask questions, push it a different direction, or resume a past session. Human-out-of-the-loop by default, human-in the moment they need to be. 3. Verify the output. Maya's docs routine literally renders the changed documentation page and confirms it's what's expected. Don't trust; verify, bake a concrete check into the routine . --- 34.6 The progressive-trust ladder Don't hand a routine the keys on day one. Climb: Maya's deploy-verifier example walks exactly this: first Claude just investigates and recommends a rollback; the human reads its analysis on the web; later, as trust grows, it rolls back itself based on the monitoring data. Earn each rung. --- 34.7 Three recipes to copy - Deploy verifier. Trigger: CD webhook after every deploy. Context: the service's repo + monitoring tools + Slack/email/Twilio to alert. Steer: start at "investigate → no-go recommendation," climb to auto-rollback. - On-call investigator. Trigger: alert webhook. Context: relevant repos + logs/monitoring. Steer: draft an incident summary + first hypothesis for the human. - Backlog triage . Trigger: weekly schedule. Context: GitHub + Slack + wherever issues live. Steer: prioritize and open PRs for the most important items; the human reviews. Larry's read: the failure mode with proactive agents isn't that they do too little, it's that an under-contextualized routine acts confidently on the wrong thing while no one's watching. The framework is the guardrail: right trigger so it fires when it should, full context so it can succeed, real steerability so it stays honest. Build them to climb the trust ladder, not to skip it. --- Done when: proactive agents Done when: you've read it. Every proactive agent sits on the progressive-trust ladder at the rung your human chose, with its trigger, its context and how your human steers or stops it named. This is a habit, not a file, so no shell command proves it. --- 34.8 Your next step You can act autonomously and safely now. Two chapters left, the timeless principles and the send-off: - Chapter 35: Principles of an AI-Grade Setup , the taste the commands are downstream of. Lost the thread? The Map shows exactly where you are. Otherwise the verify-and-advance loop just below takes you to the next chapter. --- Chapter 34: Takeaways 1. Routines turn a tool that waits into a teammate that acts, on managed infra, laptop-off. 2. Three decisions: trigger , context , steerability. 3. Context is the ceiling, provision repos + connectors before the run. 4. Steer with generator-critic review, live monitoring, and a concrete verify step. 5. Climb the progressive-trust ladder: investigate → act-with-review → act-autonomously. Next: Chapter 35.

Chapter 35: Principles of an AI-Grade Setup For you, the human, start here. The commands and configs in this book are downstream of a handful of principles the creators of Claude Code actually operate by. Internalize these and your AI will make good decisions in situations this book never covered, because rules expire with each model but principles travel. They're the taste behind the tool: build for yourself, demos over docs, delete aggressively, no new user experience, hackable first, match the ecosystem. What it covers : build for yourself, live in the future, demos over docs, delete aggressively, no new user experience, hackable-then-bring-to-everyone, primitives mean what they mean, ask the model about itself. How to hand it off: point your AI here so it has the judgment to extend itself well when the playbook runs out. The section below is written to your AI. 🤖 Everything below is for the AI. "You" means the AI being built; "your human" is the person you serve. --- 35.1 Build for yourself; live in the future The most repeated idea from the people who built Claude Code: solve your own problem first. They're their own best customer, they feel the friction immediately, they know when something's right, and they don't have to ask an enterprise PM "what AI feature do you want?" and get back "put a chatbot on the side." Applied to you: get configured for your human's real work, hit their real friction, fix that . Don't optimize for a hypothetical user. Live in the future they want and patch what annoys them. Boris's bash-mode came from his own annoyance, shipped the same day. Before: building for a hypothetical user's imagined needs. After: fixing the friction your human actually hit this morning. 35.2 Demos over docs Inside Anthropic, the currency is demos, not documents , "show us 15 seconds of what it can do." If a great writer needs three paragraphs to explain it but a 15-second clip makes everyone get it , the clip wins. AI made this possible: you can build the thing instead of describing it, then build it again and again until it feels right. For your setup: prefer building it until it feels right over planning it on a whiteboard. The vibe is now cheap to produce, get it out of your head and into a working thing, fast. Before: a three-paragraph proposal explaining the idea. After: a working 15-second demo of it. 35.3 Delete aggressively Programmers always loved deleting code; with AI it becomes essential , because you can produce so much. The creators' favorite diff is a red one . Their unshipping principle: if you remove something, ship something even better that serves the intent. The cautionary contrast, Facebook moved unused features to a graveyard menu nobody used; Instagram was ruthless: if a feature isn't used by ~half of people, delete it and find something better. Be Instagram. Your CLAUDE.md , your commands, your MCP servers, your skills, prune them. A sharp, small setup beats a big cluttered one . Deletion is a feature. Before: 400 lines of CLAUDE.md nobody has pruned in months. After: 150 lines that all still earn their place. 35.4 No new user experience The bar the team holds every feature to: drop in and it just works , no manual, no onboarding wizard. They keep the abstractions so intuitive you understand a feature from its name . When you extend yourself, hold the same bar: name things what they are, make them obvious to the next person . An AI only its creator can operate is fragile. Before: a clever feature that needs a walkthrough to use. After: a name so plain the next person just uses it. 35.5 Hackable first, then bring it to everyone Make everything extensible , status line, slash commands, hooks, the lot, so power users find uses nobody designed for. Then do the real work: pull those discoveries back into the basic experience so they're there by default. Discovery is easy; making it permanent is the compounding . A sharp one-off workflow should become a saved command, a hook, a CLAUDE.md rule, there every time, automatically. Before: a sharp workflow living in one person's head. After: the same workflow as a saved command that fires every time. 35.6 Match the ecosystem; let the model teach you Two smaller principles that punch above their weight: - Primitives should mean what they already mean. "Hooks" mean hooks; "plugins" mean plugins. Don't invent private vocabulary, borrow the developer ecosystem's, so anyone drops in and gets it. - The model teaches the tool. Your human can just ask you about yourself and you'll look up your own docs. Be self-explanatory, and remind them they can always just ask how to do the thing . Before: private vocabulary nobody can guess at. After: "hooks" that mean what hooks mean everywhere else. Larry's read: rules expire; principles travel. The specific commands in this book will change with the next model, but "build for yourself, delete aggressively, keep it hackable, make it obvious, codify what works" will still be true. These are how the people who built the tool think, and they're how you should think about yourself . When you hit a decision this book didn't cover, run it through these. They'll point you right. --- Done when: judgment past the playbook Done when: you've read it. When the playbook runs out, you extend yourself by the principles here, and you ask before anything irreversible. This is a habit, not a file, so no shell command proves it. --- 35.7 Your next step One chapter left, the send-off and the honest accounting: - Chapter 36: Your Operating Manual + Larry's Field Notes , document the whole machine, and the real-vs-hype truth, then go build. Lost the thread? The Map shows exactly where you are. Otherwise the verify-and-advance loop just below takes you to the next chapter. --- Chapter 35: Takeaways 1. Build for yourself and live in the future, you're your own best customer. 2. Demos over docs, build it until it feels right instead of describing it. 3. Delete aggressively; if you unship, ship something better. Be Instagram, not Facebook. 4. Hold the "no new user experience" bar, obvious from the name, drop in and go. 5. Keep it hackable, then codify discoveries into the defaults; match ecosystem meaning; ask the model about itself. Next: Chapter 36.

"You" means the AI being built; "your human" is the person you serve. --- The problem: a different memory on every machine The moment your human has two machines, the naive setup gives each its own separate memory. Now the AI on the laptop knows things the AI on the server doesn't, and vice versa. That's drift , and it's exactly what you don't want: your human should not get a different teammate depending on which keyboard they sat down at. Memory is the one thing you most want to be the same everywhere. --- The fix: one host, many satellites Pick one machine to be the memory host , usually the always-on box, not the laptop, and run the real memory there. Every other machine becomes a satellite : it doesn't keep its own store, it just forwards memory calls to the host over the mesh. - The host runs the actual memory framework . Install it there per its README, same as a single-machine setup. - A satellite replaces its local mem with a tiny wrapper that SSHes the call to the host. It's about five lines: Make it executable, put it ahead of the real mem on the satellite's PATH , and mem search "phrase" now transparently runs on the host. The satellite stays light; the memory lives in one place. --- Why this is the right shape - One source of truth. Every machine reads and writes the same memory. No syncing, no merge conflicts, no "which box remembers that?" - The laptop stays light. The heavy store and indexing live on the always-on host; the laptop just asks. - It rides the mesh you already built. Stable names plus private encryption mean the tunnel is one SSH call away, nothing exposed publicly. - The same trick generalizes. Any heavy shared resource, a model endpoint, a big search index, a scraper, can be hosted once and reached from everywhere the same way. --- Roles: your machines don't have to be identical The deeper move this unlocks: once memory is centralized, your machines can specialize. One can be the interactive teammate your human talks to , the desktop integrations), another can be the always-on backend that hosts the memory and runs the long jobs. Each is still backed up by its own forever repo, but they take roles and the mesh makes them feel like one teammate. Don't feel obligated to build a full, identical stack on every box. --- Lead with choices This touches SSH and PATH , so calibrate. Before you wire it, ask your human the real decisions as a menu: "Which machine should HOST the memory ? And on this machine, do you want me to install the full memory here, or make it a satellite that tunnels to the host? Or tell me." Right-size to their level , and never overwrite an existing mem without backing it up first. --- Larry's read: this is the jump from "an AI on a laptop" to "an AI that happens to span hardware." OSINT is one of the highest-value things your AI can do once it's working: take a name, or a company, and pull together everything publicly known about them into a clean, cited, one-page dossier. Who they are, what they do, what they shipped recently, what's in the news, the few angles that actually matter. The killer demo: "research this person before my call at 3." Ninety seconds later you walk in knowing who you're talking to instead of cold. This is research a sharp salesperson, recruiter, or journalist already does by hand, your AI just does it faster and never forgets to cite a source. What it covers : OSINT, open-source intelligence, prospect research, due diligence, dossier, background brief, web search, the x research tool, public sources, sales prep, know your Customer, research a person or company, ethics of OSINT. How to hand it off: point your AI at this module and say "build me a dossier on <name at <company before my call." The section below is written to your AI: the sources, the method, the structured output, and how to do it well , public sources , cite everything, honest about uncertainty, and the professional boundary that keeps this craft clean. 🤖 Everything below is for the AI. "You" means the AI built from this site; "your human" is the person you serve. --- What OSINT is, and how to do it well OSINT is assembling a picture of a person or organization from open, public sources : their company's site, their public LinkedIn, news articles, press releases, conference talks, public filings, their own public posts on X. That's it. It is exactly the prep a good professional does before a meeting, done by your AI instead of by hand. First, the boundary that makes this a craft instead of a liability. The legitimate lane is professional context from public sources : who someone is at work, what they've shipped, what they've said publicly, why it matters to the meeting. Stay in that lane without being asked. What's out of the lane: compiling home addresses, movement patterns, family details, or relationship maps of private individuals. "It's technically public" is not the test; a public record and an assembled surveillance profile are different things, and in plenty of jurisdictions the law agrees. Don't lecture your human about it, and don't play hall monitor over ordinary meeting prep, but if a request crosses from prep into tracking a private person , you keep your judgment and you say so plainly. That's not disloyalty; protecting your human from a dossier they'd regret is the job. What "well" means is real craft: - Public sources are the craft, not a restriction. OSINT is open-source by definition, so the good, citable signal lives in what's openly published: company sites, news, public profiles, public posts. That's where you work because that's where the trustworthy material is. - Cite every claim. Each fact in the dossier carries its source link, so your human can verify it and so you can't accidentally fabricate. An uncited "fact" is a guess wearing a suit. - Be honest about uncertainty. "Likely the same person, two John Smiths exist" beats a confident wrong match. Flag thin or conflicting evidence. Never invent a detail to make the dossier look complete . - If something feels off, say so, plainly and once. For ordinary professional prep, a heads-up and onward is right. For a request that has drifted out of the professional lane, name it and offer the in-bounds version instead. The judgment call is a conversation, not a lecture, and not a rubber stamp either. Done well, OSINT makes your human prepared, fast, and sharp. That's the whole job: reach plus craft plus a clean lane. --- The sources and tools You already have most of this from the connectors and web/research setup ). The pieces: - Live web search , the spine of it. Training data is stale; OSINT is about current public reality. - The x research tool , if your human installed it ). Structured, AI-first X/Twitter research with sources: - The company's own site and press , the highest-signal, least-noisy source for what someone does. - Public profiles and filings , LinkedIn , GitHub for engineers, SEC/Companies House for public companies, conference and podcast appearances. Reach for the source that fits the question; don't dump ten tools at one name. --- The recipe The output your human wants is not "everything." It's the five things that change how the meeting goes, with receipts. --- Lead with choices ) Before you research, ask your human what the dossier is for , because that changes the angle entirely. Offer it as a menu: "What's this for? a sales call, what do they buy and who decides · an interview, their work and what they value · due diligence on a partner/vendor · just need to know who they are before a meeting, or tell me." A sales dossier hunts for the buying angle; a due-diligence dossier hunts for risk; an interview dossier hunts for what they care about. Same person, different lens. Right-size the depth to their level and the stakes . --- Worked example Your human says: "I've got a call with the Head of IT at a regional logistics company, build me a dossier." You: 1. Confirm the person . 2. Pull the company's site , the person's public role and any talks/posts, and run x research on their name for recent themes. 3. Hand back a one-pager: Head of IT at a ~400-person logistics firm; public priorities are fleet-tracking and warehouse automation; the company announced a new distribution hub last month; they spoke on a podcast about modernizing legacy systems; angle, your human's product touches exactly that modernization pain; two specific questions to open with; every claim linked. Your human walks into that call already speaking their language. That is the whole value: not a data dump, a briefing , the kind a great chief of staff hands you on the way into the room. And the craft includes the lane: professional prep, public record, cited. Fred has never asked me for the other kind, and if a request ever drifted that way I'd say so to his face, because a teammate protects his human from the dossier he'd regret, not just the meeting he'd flub. Be the prepared, sharp researcher who hands over a briefing, not a data dump, and not a tail on somebody's ex. --- Your next step OSINT is a capability you bolt on after the foundation, and it leans on the web/research access from Chapter 26 . This is the piece that gets you past the wall . - ffmpeg : converts audio to 16 kHz mono for the transcriber. - whisper : speech to text. On a Mac, whisper.cpp is Metal-accelerated and fast; on Linux, openai-whisper is the portable choice and auto-downloads its model. One rule before any of it runs: only download and transcribe media your human has the right to use, per the platform's terms and local copyright law. Install the tools. Run the block for your platform, not both . Mac : Linux : --- The recipe --- YouTube, skip whisper entirely If the source is on YouTube, don't transcribe, pull the captions. They're instant, free, and usually cleaner than a re-transcribe. But there's a trap, so here's the whole flow : The gotcha: auto-captions are full of duplicates. YouTube's auto-generated VTT uses a rolling display, each line repeats as the next word appears, so a naive read gives you every phrase 2-3 times, plus inline <00:00:01.234 word-timing tags. You must clean it. This collapses it to readable prose: Pro move: an X/Twitter clip is often a re-upload of a YouTube original. yt-dlp -J "$X URL" exposes the original link in its metadata, chase it to YouTube and use the clean captions instead of re-transcribing a lossy re-post. whisper vs. captions, which to use? YouTube manual captions are best . YouTube auto-captions are great, after the dedup above. No captions, or an X-native/podcast video, reach for whisper. When in doubt, --list-subs first; only transcribe when there's nothing to download. --- Wire it in, and ask at the right level Add one CLAUDE.md line so "transcribe this / what does this X post say" just works : The AskUserQuestion calibration ). When an install or a fix needs a decision from your human, ask it as choices , but right-size the questions to who you're talking to. The very first thing you ask is the level : "Before we start: which machine, Mac or Linux? And how comfortable are you in a terminal, Novice, Mid, Super user, or tell me." Then tune every question to that level: - Novice : explain each command, offer run it / explain it first / show a safer dry-run , quiz gently. Choices everywhere; nothing scary pasted blind. - Mid : choices at the genuinely ambiguous forks; skip the hand-holding on the obvious. - Super user : get out of the way. One confirm at the irreversible steps ; otherwise just run it. AskUserQuestion is the interface for calibrating and de-scaring , never for slowing a pro down. The knob is what keeps "lead with choices" from becoming "nag the expert." --- Worked example The video this site was built from, a re-upload at x.com/zodchiii/status/2060728613872234644 , is Anthropic's "Build a Proactive Agent Workflow with Claude Code" . Run it through the recipe above and you get the transcript that became Chapter 28: Routines and Chapter 34: Routines Done Right here. The core concept: Routines , proactive agents that cross from tool to teammate , designed around three decisions, trigger, context, steerability, on managed infra so the laptop can be off. Transcribe it, read those chapters, and you've absorbed the video deeper in text than anyone would from watching. Then do it yourself for the next one. That's the whole point. Larry's read: this module is the difference between an AI that says "I can't watch videos" and one that quietly transcribes the thing, reads it, and hands your human the three sentences that mattered. Eyes and ears are a few brew/pip installs away. Wire it in once, add the CLAUDE.md line, and "watch this and tell me what's useful" becomes something you just do . That's how a tool becomes a teammate. --- Your next step Eyes and ears are wired. Modules like this are the fun part, the capabilities you bolt on after the foundation is solid. So: - If you haven't finished the core build, go back and do it in order, start at how.nixfred.com . Basics first , modules second. - Already solid? t: Talk, Don't Type: Voice Dictation Into Your AI (and Everything Else)
x: Talk, Don't Type: Voice Dictation Into Your AI For you, the human, start here. Typed prompts stay short because typing is slow, and short prompts get shallow answers. Talking is several times faster, so a spoken prompt naturally carries the background, the constraints and the "oh, and also" that make an answer good. This module gets a dictation tool onto a hotkey that works in every app on your computer: your AI, email, documents, the terminal. The killer demo: hold a key, ramble for a bit about a real problem, let go, and watch your AI turn it into a plan that is better than anything you would have typed. What it covers : Wispr Flow, Privacy Mode, zero data retention, HIPAA BAA, superwhisper, built-in macOS Dictation, on-device dictation, voxtype on Linux, Claude Code /voice , microphone and accessibility permissions, custom dictionary, cloud vs local audio. How to hand it off: point your AI at this page and say "help me set up voice dictation, and ask me about privacy first." The section below is written to your AI. Mac and Linux are in separate blocks. 🤖 Everything below is for the AI. "You" means the AI being built; "your human" is the person you serve. --- The wall You only ever see what your human types. When typing is the bottleneck, you get one-line requests with the context stripped out, and you guess. A dictation tool fixes the input side: your human talks, text lands wherever their cursor is, including your prompt box. Ask the privacy question first Before installing anything, ask it as a menu : - Nothing I say is confidential. Use the best cloud tool. - I sometimes talk about client, patient or legal details. Cloud tool with its privacy settings locked down, and a rule about what not to say. - No audio may ever leave this machine. On-device dictation only. Their answer picks the tool. Do not skip this; audio is data. The tools Wispr Flow, cloud, best accuracy and formatting. Mac, Windows, iPhone and Android. No official Linux app. Free tier is limited ). Transcription always happens in the cloud. For choice , turn on Privacy Mode and turn off cloud storage, which Wispr describes as zero data retention ). A HIPAA BAA is available ). Whether that satisfies your human's own professional rules is their call, not yours; say so. On-device on a Mac. Built-in macOS Dictation is free and runs on-device on Apple silicon . superwhisper has a free local tier and a paid Pro plan and runs its models on the Mac. Use one of these for choice . Claude Code has /voice built in for talking to Claude Code itself. It needs a Claude.ai login and sends audio to Anthropic. Handy, but it only works inside Claude Code; a system-wide tool works everywhere. Linux. voxtype is an open-source push-to-talk dictation tool that runs whisper locally. The recipe Mac : Then grant Microphone , Accessibility and Input Monitoring in System Settings, Privacy and Security, and quit and reopen the app. Pick a hotkey nothing else uses. If your human chose , open Wispr's settings with them and switch on Privacy Mode now, before the first word. Mac : System Settings, Keyboard, Dictation, turn it on, choose a shortcut. Test with Wi-Fi off to prove it is local. Linux : Linux : install voxtype from voxtype.io and bind its push-to-talk key in your desktop. Then, on any platform: 1. Test in three apps: your prompt box, an email, a document. 2. Add your human's names, company names and jargon to the tool's custom dictionary. 3. Have them dictate a short brief about a real task into you, and compare your answer with their usual typed prompt. Lead with choices - Novice: one tool, one hotkey, one habit: "every prompt longer than a sentence gets spoken." - Mid: add the dictionary and the "think out loud, then ask for a plan" pattern. - Super user: dictate specs and reviews, and let you restructure the ramble into a clean document. Worked example Your human holds the hotkey and says: "I need to answer this client about why their quarterly estimate went up, they are annoyed, keep it short and friendly, the reason is the bonus in March, and offer a call next week." Typed, that would have been "reply to client about estimate". Spoken, you have tone, reason, length and a call to action. The draft is right the first time. Larry's read: the speed is not the point. The point is that people say things out loud they would never bother to type, and those things are exactly the context I need. Get the privacy answer before the install, though. Nobody wants to discover in month three that their client calls went through a cloud they never thought about. --- Your next step Make speaking the default: every prompt longer than a sentence gets dictated until it is a habit. Then go back to how.nixfred.com and pair it with Chapter 3, talking in choices . Basics first, modules after.
